newsitem.title: JAPAN: FEATURE - Japan stewardesses suffer in unfriendly skies.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Japan stewardesses suffer in unfriendly skies.

text.p: The Japanese, normally thought of around the world as the epitome of politeness and good manners, are lately proving somewhat less restrained in the air.
The victims are Japanese airline stewardesses who are increasingly having to endure insults, humiliations and even beatings by drunken or stressed-out passengers.

Toshio Takahashi, a spokesman for the country's largest carrier, Japan Air Lines Co Ltd (JAL), said reports of attacks and abuse against cabin crews had almost tripled in 1996 to 40 cases, from an average of 15 cases in the two previous years.
Statistics are not available for attacks so far in 1997, but stewardess unions say they see no signs of incidents abating.
The attacks include being stabbed with pens, punched in the face, grabbed by the bottom or breasts, and being forced to get down on hands and knees to apologise to drunken passengers.
"Troublesome incidents are up 2.7-fold, ranging from fights between passengers in which staff get involved, to physical attacks to sexual harassment," Takahashi told Reuters.
A BETTER CLASS OF LOUT

Unlike most foreign airlines, who mainly run into passenger trouble with drunken tourists or sports teams in economy class, Japan's worst offenders appear to be middle-aged executives of major firms flying first or business class, Takahashi said.
Former stewardess and now travel writer Kumiko Kaneda said executives were under extreme pressures now due to cost-cutting restructuring and were taking it out on flight staff.
"Three years ago inflight trouble was bad, but it's worse now. Middle-aged executives get pressure from above and below, so when they come on the plane they let it all out," she said.
"They're often very used to flying and just think they can act like they're at home. They also have the mistaken impression that just because someone is younger, they can push them around."
GETTING HIGH AT THREE TIMES THE SPEED
High altitude triples the effect of alcohol -- a major factor in cases of unruly behaviour, JAL's Takahashi said.
"Drink is a major cause -- you get drunk three times as fast at high altitude and a lot of people don't know that," he said.

"It seems to be a peculiarly Japanese thing. When Japanese get drunk at a drinking session after work they just let loose. Its a business tradition. So when they get drunk somewhere else, they think they're in the same situation," he said.
Japan Air System Co Ltd spokesman Koiichi Iwamoto said incidents were more common on longer flights.
"On the longer flights there is more time to drink so this kind of thing seems to occur more often," he said.
Flight attendants want airlines to mount strict checks to prevent drunken or difficult passengers from boarding.
"If they just stopped them getting on the plane our lives would be a lot easier," a 20-year serving stewardess said.
RISING HOLIDAY FLIGHT MAYHEM
A spokeswoman for "Stewardess" a flight magazine with a circulation of 90,000, said a steady increase in package holidays also meant more rowdy groups for stewardesses to deal with.
"There's a likelihood of more trouble on the long flights where there are many passengers, like to Honolulu. They drink a lot and can just generally run amok," she said.
People vomiting over fellow passengers or getting into fights are a common problem, she said.
But Keiichi Tsujino, a spokesman for Japanese tour operator JTB, said big airlines themselves were partly to blame for using drinks as an incentive to customers.
"One of the reasons why people get so drunk is that some airlines give wine and other alcoholic drinks freely in order to woo passengers to their flights," he said.
However, lack of consideration for inferiors in Japanese society was to blame for bullying by passengers, a veteran steward said.
"THE CUSTOMER IS GOD"

"People think they can get away with the sort of thing which just wouldn't be tolerated in the West. It's a basic lack of respect. We're not slaves, although you might get that impression from the way some of them abuse us verbally," he said.
"It happens several times a month. Recently, a passenger who couldn't get the purser's eye when she was busy selling duty free goods started shouting and calling her an 'Old Bag'."
However, unwritten company and social etiquette means staff have to grin and bear harassment and sexual abuse.
"Because of the way things are, we just suffer in silence," the steward said.

A well-known case in which a whole flight crew prostrated themselves in the gangway to placate a drunken and truculent passenger was not taking the Japanese adage "The customer is God" too far, JAL's Takahashi said.
"Getting down on your hands and knees is one way to deal with a potentially dangerous situation in such a closed space. You can't call the police after all," he said.
